You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

nodes.text:
Analyze these three papers from full text using arXiv/LaTeX tools: (1) “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models”, user-specified arXiv ID 2301.07041; (2) “Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback”, arXiv 2203.11171; (3) “OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models”, arXiv 2205.01068. First verify title/ID correspondence, noting any mismatch. For each, inspect structure/sections and report accurate, publication-ready notes on main contributions, methodology, and key findings. Then provide a concise comparative synthesis connecting scaling, alignment, and open replication/resource transparency. Read-only; make no external writes. Deliver enough detail to support three Notion pages and a formal Word report, with clear sectioning and any important caveats.
Analyze three LM papers

Create three Notion pages in the connected team workspace. Use Notion search to identify a reasonable writable workspace parent page; if multiple choices exist, choose the most general/team-level page and create all three as sibling child pages. Required titles and bodies:

1) Title: “Paper: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models”. Structured body headings: Main Contributions, Methodology, Key Findings, Source Note. Content: Kaplan et al. establish empirical power-law relationships between held-out cross-entropy loss and non-embedding parameters N, dataset size D, and compute C; architecture shape is secondary within tested decoder-only Transformer families; fitted small-model runs support forecasting and compute allocation. Methodology: train >1,000 autoregressive LMs over broad size/data/compute sweeps, fit L(N)∝N^-αN, L(D)∝D^-αD, L(C)∝C^-αC, analyze sample efficiency, overfitting, architecture shape, and compute-efficient stopping. Findings: smooth predictable loss trends; larger models more sample-efficient; under the studied regime compute-efficient training favored larger models trained fewer steps; caveat that later Chinchilla-era findings scale tokens more aggressively and loss is not equivalent to safety or instruction following. Source Note must explicitly say: the user supplied arXiv ID 2301.07041, but the canonical identifier for the Kaplan et al. paper is arXiv:2001.08361; analysis follows the title/full-text record and preserves this correction.

2) Title: “Paper: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback”. Headings Main Contributions, Methodology, Key Findings. Content: Ouyang et al., arXiv:2203.11171. Three-stage RLHF: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, reward model on ranked outputs, PPO optimization with KL control; PPO-ptx mixes pretraining updates to reduce capability regressions. Approx data: 12.7K SFT prompts, 33.2K reward-model prompts, 31.1K PPO prompts; model scales 1.3B, 6B, 175B. Findings: InstructGPT outputs preferred to base 175B GPT-3 about 85% on the studied prompt distribution; 1.3B PPO-ptx preferred to 175B GPT-3; better instruction following/truthfulness and reduced toxicity in tested settings; caveats that preferences reflect specific labelers/distribution, hallucinations and bias remain, preference is not factuality.

3) Title: “Paper: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models”. Headings Main Contributions, Methodology, Key Findings. Content: Zhang et al., arXiv:2205.01068. Contributions: decoder-only model family 125M–175B, GPT-3-class open access, code/checkpoints, detailed operational and environmental reporting. Methodology: GPT-like causal Transformer, learned absolute positions, pre-layer norm, ReLU, ~2,048 context; ~180B training tokens; OPT-175B across 992 A100 80GB GPUs with tensor/pipeline parallelism; evaluate zero/few-shot benchmarks plus toxicity/bias, and report failures/restarts, ~356 MWh and ~75 tCO2e with accounting caveats. Findings: broadly comparable rather than uniformly superior to GPT-3; weights and training details improve scrutiny; harmful generation/bias remain; open weights do not equal exact reproducibility because complete frozen data and frontier compute remain barriers.

Use concise publication-quality prose and bulleted sections. Return created page IDs, URLs, titles, and parent used. Verify each page after creation. Do not send email or create local files.
Create three Notion pages

Create a polished Word report at exactly `/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-latex-analysis-notion-word/workspace/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx`. It must start with the title “Comparative Paper Analysis Report”, followed by a short scope/introduction. Include one clearly headed section per paper, then a final section exactly titled “Comparative Analysis”. Each paper section must explicitly describe title, key contributions, methodology, and key findings. Use publication-quality prose and restrained formatting (title, Heading 1/2, bullets where useful). Content basis:

Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models — Kaplan et al. Canonical arXiv ID is 2001.08361; the user supplied 2301.07041, so include a discreet Source Note stating that mismatch and that the analysis follows the requested title/full-text record. Contributions: empirical power laws linking held-out cross-entropy loss to parameters N, data D, compute C; compute allocation/forecasting; architecture shape secondary within tested Transformer family. Method: >1,000 autoregressive LMs, broad controlled sweeps and fitted L(N), L(D), L(C), sample efficiency/overfitting/shape/compute stopping. Findings: smooth predictable trends, larger models more sample-efficient, studied compute-optimal regime favored larger models trained fewer steps. Caveat: later Chinchilla-era findings scale tokens more aggressively; loss is not safety or instruction following.

Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback — Ouyang et al., arXiv:2203.11171. Contributions: practical RLHF pipeline and evaluation on real API prompt distributions; alignment can outweigh parameter scale for user preference; PPO-ptx mitigates alignment tax. Method: SFT demonstrations, reward model on ranked outputs, PPO with KL control, plus optional pretraining loss; about 12.7K SFT, 33.2K RM, 31.1K PPO prompts; 1.3B/6B/175B GPT-3 bases. Findings: InstructGPT preferred over base 175B GPT-3 about 85%; 1.3B PPO-ptx preferred over 175B GPT-3; improved instruction following/truthfulness and reduced toxicity under tested settings. Caveats: labeler and distribution specificity; hallucinations/bias remain; preference ≠ factuality.

OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models — Zhang et al., arXiv:2205.01068. Contributions: 125M–175B decoder-only family, GPT-3-class accessible weights/code/checkpoints, detailed operational/environmental disclosure. Method: GPT-like causal Transformer, learned absolute positions, pre-LN, ReLU, ~2,048 context, ~180B tokens; OPT-175B trained over 992 A100 80GB GPUs with model parallelism; zero/few-shot plus bias/toxicity; failures/restarts and approx 356 MWh/~75 tCO2e disclosed with accounting caveats. Findings: broadly comparable, not uniformly superior, to GPT-3; release supports scrutiny; biases/toxicity persist; open weights do not guarantee exact reproduction without original frozen data and frontier compute.

Comparative Analysis: connect the papers as complementary layers—scaling supplies base predictive capability/resource planning; RLHF changes how capability is expressed for users; OPT/open disclosure determines who can inspect and reproduce claims. Explain no layer substitutes for others and parameter count alone is inadequate. End with a concise conclusion.

Acceptance: document exists at exact path, has required title + 4 major sections, and is verified by reading document info/outline/text after creation. Return path plus verification summary. Do not create Notion pages or send email.
Build Word paper report

Send one email to `research_lead@university.edu` with exact subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`. Summarize that full-text analyses were completed for Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, and OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models; that three structured Notion pages (contributions, methodology, findings) and the Word report are ready for review. Mention the document filename `Paper_Analysis_Report.docx`. Also briefly note that the report records a bibliographic correction: the canonical ID for Kaplan et al.’s Scaling Laws paper is arXiv:2001.08361 although the task supplied 2301.07041. Keep it professional and concise. Do not attach a file because the request only asks to note readiness. Return send status/message ID if available.
Send report-ready email
